sections.h: 'No longer keeping the Sabbath': Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1
sections.b:
On his way to martyrdom in the reign of Trajan (98-117, as Lake dates it), Ignatius of Antioch wrote to the church at Magnesia: 'If, then, those who lived in the old ways came to a new hope, no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day], on which our life also rose through him and through his death, which some deny ...' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1), and the sentence ends with a question: 'how will we be able to live without him?' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2). It is the line most often quoted from the generation after the apostles in the argument over the two days.

Three things are argued. (1) The text. The Greek has the adjective alone, 'the Lord's', with no word for 'day' (the brackets mark the supplied word); the one Greek manuscript adds 'life' ('living by the Lord's life'), which Lake, Lightfoot and Zahn leave out with the Latin and Armenian, and which Fritz Guy (1964) argued should stay. (2) The subject. Lightfoot reads 'those who lived in the old ways' as Jewish believers who had stopped keeping the Sabbath; Guy reads them as the prophets of 8:2, so that 'keeping the Sabbath' stands for a legalistic way of life. (3) The force. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes the verse for Sunday replacing the Sabbath's 'ceremonial observance' (Catechism 2175); Guy concludes that it 'can not at the present time properly be introduced as evidence' that the Lord's day was kept, nor ruled out as an allusion to it.

The word Ignatius uses for keeping the Sabbath, sabbatizō, is not in the New Testament; Hebrews 4:9 has the noun: 'a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people'. The full phrase 'the Lord's day' is Revelation 1:10. Each church's teaching is on the cards at Revelation 1:10, Exodus 20 and Colossians 2.

common: Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1 shows that in Ignatius's day Christians in Asia had left the Sabbath for the Lord's day.
uncommon: The verse is about two ways of life, legalism and life in Christ, and says nothing certain about days (Fritz Guy, 1964).

sections.b:
Ignatius uses Paul's words. 'If we are still living by Judaism to this day, we admit that we have not received grace' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:1); 'It is out of place to talk of Jesus Christ and live in the Jewish way' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:3), with the verb of Galatians 2:14. He calls the teaching 'old myths' and 'the bad yeast', and sets the prophets on Christ's side: they 'lived by Christ Jesus' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2).

Who held it is not said. Lake: 'it is disputed whether he means that this was an evil found in docetic circles, or that it was a danger threatening the church from other directions.' Lightfoot links it with those who denied Christ's death (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1; 11:1): 'a Docetic Judaism'. Fritz Guy reads it as an attitude, legalism, more than a party. Ignatius writes to Christians about Christians, and says he does not know that any at Magnesia hold it (Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1).

sections.b: Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:3 sets two new words side by side: 'Christianity did not put its faith in Judaism. Judaism put its faith in Christianity'. The letter is written to a church, about practices among Christians that Ignatius opposes, and he says he does not know that any Magnesians follow them (Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1). It also says the prophets 'lived by Christ Jesus' and were persecuted for it (Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2). Lightfoot's comment on the verse, that Christianity was 'a larger and better dispensation than Judaism', reads it as a comparison of the two faiths. This page gives the later history of Christian texts used against Jews.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:1-2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:3; Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1

sections.b: Written from Smyrna (Ignatius to the Magnesians 15:1) to a church near Ephesus that had sent its overseer Damas, two elders and a deacon to meet him (Ignatius to the Magnesians 2:1). It asks for unity with a young overseer (Ignatius to the Magnesians 3:1), sets the overseer 'in the place of God' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1), and warns against living 'by Judaism', with the much-quoted 'no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day]' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1) and the earliest known uses of the word 'Christianity' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:1-3, as Lightfoot says).

sections.h: The overseer, the elders and the deacons at Magnesia
sections.b: Magnesia's delegation to Ignatius 'comprised all orders of the ministry' (Lightfoot): the overseer Damas, the elders Bassus and Apollonius, the deacon Zotion (Ignatius to the Magnesians 2:1). Ignatius asks the church to respect its overseer though he is young, as the elders do, deferring 'to the Father of Jesus Christ, the overseer of all' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 3:1). He asks them to do everything 'with the overseer presiding in the place of God, and the elders in the place of the council of the apostles' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1; two witnesses read 'as a type of God'), calls the elders 'that well-woven spiritual crown' round the overseer (Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:1), and asks that nothing be done without the overseer and the elders (Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:1). The Catechism of the Catholic Church cites 6:1 with Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1 (Catechism 1549); Lightfoot called the letters' language 'extravagant exaltation of the episcopal office', explained by 'the needs and distractions of the age'.

sections.h: Zotion and the deacons at Magnesia
sections.b: Ignatius calls the deacon Zotion his 'fellow slave' and praises him for being subject to the overseer and the elders (Ignatius to the Magnesians 2:1). The deacons, 'dearest to me', are 'entrusted with the ministry of Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1), the word diakonia behind their name. Lake thinks the sentence about them was left unfinished.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 2:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:1

sections.h: The elders 'in the place of the council of the apostles'
sections.b: In Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1 the elders preside 'in the place of the council of the apostles', while the overseer stands 'in the place of God'. The picture is of a council round its head, as the Twelve round Christ; Ignatius does not say here that the overseer or the elders succeed the apostles in office. The cards at 2 Timothy 2 and Acts 1 give each church's teaching on succession.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1

sections.h: 'His Word, who came forth from silence'
sections.b: Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2 calls Jesus Christ God's 'Word, who came forth from silence'. The Greek manuscript and the Latin read instead 'his eternal Word, not coming forth from silence', which Lake and 'recent editors' regard as a change made 'due to fear of Gnostic theories'. Lightfoot reads the phrase of the incarnation: God, silent until then, spoke his Word in Christ, as in Romans 16:25, 'the mystery kept in silence for long ages'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1; John 1:1; Romans 16:25; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1

sections.h: Before the ages, and at the end: Ignatius to the Magnesians
sections.b: Ignatius to the Magnesians confesses the Son who 'was with the Father before the ages and appeared at the end' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1), who 'came forth from the one Father, was with the one, and went back to the one' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:2), and who is God's 'Word, who came forth from silence' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2). Against those who deny it, it lists 'the birth and the suffering and the resurrection, which took place in the time when Pontius Pilate was governor', all done 'truly and surely' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1; John 16:28

sections.h: 'He came and raised them': Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2
sections.b: Ignatius writes of the prophets: 'the one they rightly waited for came and raised them from the dead' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2). Lake's footnote takes it 'more probably' as the belief 'that Jesus by the descent into Hades set free, and took into Paradise, the righteous dead', found in later writings such as the Gospel of Nicodemus. Lake's margin gives Matthew 27:52; Lightfoot points to 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 and traces the belief through Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hermas and Clement of Alexandria.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2; Matthew 27:52-53; 1 Peter 3:19; 1 Peter 4:6

sections.b: For Ignatius the prophets 'lived by Christ Jesus' and were persecuted for it, 'inspired by his grace' to convince the disobedient that there is one God (Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2); they 'were his disciples in the Spirit and looked for him as their teacher' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2). Lightfoot compares 1 Peter 1:10-11, where 'the Spirit of Christ within them' bore witness in advance.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2; 1 Peter 1:10-11

sections.h: Pilate in Ignatius to the Magnesians
sections.b: Ignatius dates 'the birth and the suffering and the resurrection' to 'the time when Pontius Pilate was governor', and insists they were done 'truly and surely' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1), as 1 Timothy 6:13 recalls Christ's confession 'in front of Pontius Pilate'.

Ignatius to the Magnesians touches the denial of Christ's real death twice: the Lord's death, 'which some deny' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1; Lightfoot: 'The allusion is to Docetism'), and the birth, suffering and resurrection done 'truly and surely' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1). Lightfoot holds that the same teachers kept Jewish practices; Lake says this is disputed.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1

sections.h: Son, Father and Spirit in Ignatius to the Magnesians
sections.b: Ignatius wishes the Magnesians to prosper 'in the Son and the Father and in the Spirit' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:1), and grounds their submission in Christ's to the Father and the apostles' 'to Christ and to the Father' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:2; the Greek manuscript and the Latin add 'and to the Spirit').
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:1-2; Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14

sections.b: Ignatius to the Magnesians warns against 'other opinions' and 'old myths that are of no use' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:1), against meetings held apart from the overseer (Ignatius to the Magnesians 4:1) and against 'the hooks of empty conceit' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1), but says he does not know that any Magnesians are 'like this'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 4:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 8:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1; 1 Timothy 1:4; Titus 1:14

sections.b: 'All of you, run together as into one temple of God, as to one altar, to one Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:2). The letter's word for the church's life is union: 'one prayer, one request, one mind, one hope' when they meet in one place (Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:1), as Ephesians 4:4-6 lists 'one body and one Spirit'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:1-2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 1:2; Ephesians 4:4-6

sections.b: 'The Ephesians greet you from Smyrna, the place I am writing to you from', 'together with Polycarp, overseer of the Smyrnaeans' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 15:1).

Ignatius asks the Magnesians to pray for 'the church in Syria', his own church at Antioch, that it 'may be counted worthy to be refreshed with dew through your church' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 14:1).

Ignatius to the Magnesians 15:1 names Polycarp, 'overseer of the Smyrnaeans', with Ignatius at Smyrna; Lake's English counts him among those who refreshed the prisoner, while Lightfoot would 'perhaps' join him to the greeting.
